title: The tower that insists on leaning
text: The Leaning Tower of Pisa was a mistake from the third storey up. Construction began in 1173 on ground that turned out to be {{1}} — soft clay and sand that could not carry the weight — and by the time builders reached the top, a century later, the tower was already {{2}}. Ever since, the tower has conducted a long negotiation with gravity. Engineers {{3}} it in the 1830s by digging a walkway around the base; Mussolini's engineers {{4}} it worse by pouring concrete into the foundations. By 1990 the lean had {{5}} five and a half degrees, and the tower was closed. The rescue that followed is a masterpiece of {{6}}: forty-one extraction tubes removed small amounts of soil from the northern side, letting the tower {{7}} half a degree — deliberately, over years — to an angle declared safe for the next three centuries. The committee {{8}} straightening it completely. Tourists come to Pisa for the error; a vertical tower would be a fine piece of Romanesque architecture, and no photograph at all.

gaps.explanation: 'ground that turned out to be yielding' — soft, giving way; yawn = open wide (a gap yawned).
'the tower was already tilting' — leaning to one side; tussle = struggle.
'engineers aggravated it' — made the lean worse; aggrandise = make something seem grander.
'made it worse' — the standard collocation; mend = repair, which would be the opposite of the outcome.
'the lean had hit five and a half degrees' — reached that mark; hoist = lift with ropes.
'a masterpiece of patience' — moving millimetres over years; patients are people in hospital, the sound-alike.
'letting the tower ease half a degree' — shift gradually and gently; erase = rub out.
'the committee declined straightening it completely' — chose not to; incline = lean, the same root as the tower's problem.
